newsitem.title: SPAIN: INSTANT VIEW - Spain cuts key rate to 5.75 pct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Spain cuts key rate to 5.75 pct.

text.p: Following are comments from economists after the Bank of Spain cut its key money rate 25 basis points to 5.75 percent.
The Bank of Spain last cut on January 16. It started the lower rates cycle on December 22 1995 when the key money market rate was reduced to 9.00 percent from 9.25 percent.
"I was surprised because it seems to me it is based only on good February CPI, shrugging off other things such as the peseta's weakness.
We'll see the reaction in the market in the following days..it could be the last time they cut"
CARMEN HERNANSANZ, ECONOMIST AT MERRILL LYNCH ESPANA

"The Bank of Spain has responded with its usual caution and has only cut 25 basis points. Although most CPI components are performing well, services have a resistance at 3.4/3.5 percent and this invites caution. Also the peseta has gone through episodes of volatility. But this doesn't mean that it won't carry on cutting, as inflation will continue to decline and the Bank of Spain could cut again in May or even before, depending on new improvements in CPI.
I think the Bank of Spain has earned its reputation with caution so, if it cuts rates, it's because it is reasonably satisfied with prices and this generates confidence in the markets"
JUAN MIELGO, ECONOMIST AT BANK OF AMERICA, MADRID

"(The central bank) had economic reasons to cut even more, at around 50 basis points, but at the same time EMU jitters and peseta's weakness were suggesting they hold rates. So they cut 25 basis points which is neutral.
From an economic point of view they have a plenty of room to cut more, I'd say around 100 basis points more. But if they cut they will do it by no more the 25 basis points each time.
Bonos won't react very positively, because of the international scenario."
ALFREDO URRUTIA, ECONOMIST AT SOCIETE GENERALE

"The Bank of Spain's opted for caution with a cut of just one quarter of a point because with a half point cut it would have used up all its current leeway and probably there would have been some profit-taking (in the market).

The current peseta level didn't stop the cut because we can't say the peseta is weak at levels of between 84.85/85.00 to the mark. At the same time the risk of importing inflation because of the rise in the price of crude and the dollar is also a risk for the countries around us." -- Madrid newsroom +341 585 2160
